Question: Can hypertension medicines be stopped after high blood pressure is under control?
Answer: No. Blood pressure drugs are not a cure. They lower blood pressure by antagonizing the rise in blood pressure, but do not change the underlying pathology behind high blood pressure. Arteriosclerosis, plaque in the arteries, whose deposition increases with age, is associated with high blood pressure. Although its build-up can be slowed down by adopting a healthful lifestyle, once established, little can be done to clear the plaque. Plaque reduces compliance of the arteries, which compliance is a physiological mechanism used by the body to regulate blood pressure. Besides, blood pressure regulation has a timeline above which the neuronal feedback from blood to the brain to make these adjustments is lost. Tissue perfusion or blood flow is the prime goal of the pumping heart. Once compliance is lost through arteriosclerosis, the heart attempts to pump much harder to achieve its goal. However, met with obstruction, from stiff and narrowed blood vessels, less blood leaves the heart and the stroke volume falls, as the heart rate and total peripheral resistance rise. Tissue perfusion falls even much lower. Blood pressure is thus reset at a higher level in a bid to imaintain optimal cardiac output, blood flow and tissue perfusion. High blood pressure drugs pharmacologically dilate the stiff blood arteries and/or slow the heart and/or reduce blood volume to increase arterial compliance, blood flow and tissue perfusion. If you stop taking the drug(s) that had lowered your blood pressure, and with this pathology still in place, blood pressure rises back up again. And sometimes to a much higher value. That said for essential hypertenstion, high blood pressure due to a known, correctable, cause like kidney failure, can go away once the underlying kidney dysfunction has been corrected, but stopping treatment without the correction will not help. Lifestyle changes like exercise, low salt intake and weight loss may lower blood pressure by reducing the burden on blood vessels and the heart and this will reduce the need for drugs in borderline hypertension cases.

Question: How does the SA node work as a pacemaker?
Answer: The sinoatrial node (SAN) has ‘funny channels’ which are permeable to potassium and sodium ions. These channels are activated by hyperpolarization and gated by cyclic nucleotides, and are understandably referred to as hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels. As the action potential (signal) generated by depolarization and then repolarization ends with hyperpolarization, just before rectification, these HCN (funny) channels open to allow in potassium and sodium ions for the next depolarization/repolarization/hyperpolarization events of signal formation, and the repeat cycle continues to make subsequent signals. This fact gives credence to the qualification of HCN channels as hyperpolarization-activated and the appellation funny channels for being activated by negative voltage. The cycling through the activation of funny channels by hyperpolarization allows for automaticity or spontaneity of the pacemaker. The pacemaker gives the heartbeat a rate of 100 - 120 beats per minute but the normal resting heart rate is lower (about 72 beats per minute) due to a baseline parasympathetic tone or influence. Cyclic AMP (cAMP), coupled to the beta-1 adrenergic receptors for noradrenaline that is released by sympathetic nervous system activation, speeds the opening of these channels to increase the heart rate, and cyclic GMP (cGMP), coupled to muscarinic receptors, M2, for acetylcholine released by the parasympathetic vagus nerve, slows its opening to slow down the heart rate. Cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP are cyclic nucleotides, hence the qualification of the HCN channel as cyclic nucleotide-gated.

A liquid meal or a beverage, high in refined sugar, is the most common culprit. This can happen when the pancreas responds slowly to rising blood sugar levels and doesn't release enough insulin early in the meal. After the meal, blood sugar levels rise, which can trigger the pancreas to overreact and release too much insulin later on. This extra insulin can cause blood sugar levels to drop below normal, even after the body has digested the meal's sugars. It should be differentiated from diabetic hypoglycemia that may occur in diabetics after an insulin overdose injection. Non-reactive hypoglycemia occurs when you have not eaten, when your calorific intake is low such as in fasting or starvation. It typically occurs if you skip a meal, drink too much alcohol, or exercise more than usual.

A heart attack usually results from the blockade of a coronary artery by a clot (thrombus or embolus), derived from the breakage of an indwelling plaque (atheroma), usually by hypertension, or stems from coronary artery spasm. A heart attack can result in ventricular fibrillation, a rapid and haphazard electrical activity that makes the heart to stop functioning as a pump, referred to as a pulseless heart or cardiac arrest which, without a timely mechanical resuscitation (CPR), hands-on or device-assisted and sometimes with pharmacological intervention, will lead to death. Other forms or causes of cardiac arrest include supraventricular tachycardia, pulseles electrical activity (PEA), severe bradycardia, and asystole which is the condition when the heart completely stops beating.

Fast glycolytic, fast twitch or Type IIx, fibers have relatively fast contractions and primarily use anaerobic glycolysis. The faster ATP can be produced by respiration, the faster and the more sustained the muscle fiber will contract after the activation of the motor neuron by the brain. You can increase the force of contraction of the muscle by either recruiting more muscle fibers or increasing the rate at which motor neurons fire, and more often you do both. When you increase the rate of firing of motor neurons to increase the effort put against a heavy load, motor neuron signals synchronize, making all the muscle fibers to contract at the same time and relax at the same time. This leads to jerks, trembling, tremors, shakes or spasms. It is normal for heavy loads, but if it occurs for minor loads, you may be having flabby unconditioned muscles where the the cross-bridge between the actin and the myosin myofilaments (within myofibrils) are weak and detach faster or at a high frequency to produce tremors. If your glucose levels are low, you may not be able to produce enough force to keep the myosin over actin to sustain contraction and considering the overfiring of the sympathetic nervous system in hypoglycemia to release stored glucose, this sympathetic action in the skeletal muscle will cause tremors. So, condition your muscles, and make sure you are well nourished in order to try and offset this phenomenon, for you will not need to overly raise the frequency of motor neuron firing to generate force and risk synchronizing signals and producing tremors or jerks.

Question: Why do you inhale?
Answer: You inhale to establish enough blood oxygen saturation that is going to meet the metabolic needs of the body at each given time. The more the activity level, the increased the metabolic needs, the higher the oxygen demands, and the more heavily and rapidly you will breathe to increase your oxygen intake. Oxygen is the last electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. This electron transport chain is responsible for oxidative phosporylation, the generation of an electromotive force, derived from the proton gradient that is produced by the proton pump, which produces ATP. ATP is the energy currency of the body which is needed for cellular, mental and physical or physiological activities of the body. You can also inhale forcefully to detect scents, or take in powder, aerosol, drugs (medicinal or recreational drugs).

Question: What are the reasons for facial darkening as a person ages?
Answer: Direct exposure to sunlight tans the body. The face is generally more exposed to the rays of ultraviolet A rays, UVA, not absorbed by the ozone layer of the atmosphere, and which penetrate the skin more than UVB, causing tanning. As you age, you build up cumulative doses of tanning from UVA that give rise to facial darkening. This tanning, increased production and oxidation of melanin, is a protective effect to prevent the damaging effects of exposure to UVA rays. In fact, the increased tanning correlates with increased incidence of DNA damage and risks of skin cancer (melanoma, basal cell cancer and squamous cell cancer). UVA is the main cause of photoaging (premature aging). The UVB rays are more damaging but do not penetrate the skin so much because they are reflected away and scattered out of the skin, being stronger. They damage the upper, superficial skin layers, causing sunburns. The UVC rays, the strongest but least penetrating rays, are mostly absorbed by the ozone layer of the upper atmosphere, do not the reach the earth and hence are harmless.

Question: What happens to excess oxygen and carbon dioxide in our bodies during respiration? Why does this not cause harm to us?
Answer: Oxygen released from hemoglobin in the red cell into body tissue is sent (diffuses) to the mitochondrial electron transport chain where it accepts an electron and then combines with the proton from NADH/FADH2 to form water or it is used for fat oxidation in beta oxidation within the cytoplasm (peroxisome) and in the mitochondria. The electron comes from NADH and FADH2 arising from the Kreb’s cycle and beta oxidation. Carbon dioxide is produced from decarboxylation reactions taking place in the Kreb’s cycle within the mitochondrial matrix after glycolysis happening in the cytosol or following beta oxidation in the cytosol and within the mitochondrial matrix. The carbon dioxide (85%) dissolves in water to form carbonic acid which then dissociates into a proton and the bicarbonate ion in the presence of carbonic anhydrase within the red blood cell. The proton binds to hemoglobin while the bicarbonate ion is transported dissolved in blood plasma. Some of the carbon dioxide (10%) binds directly with hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin. When the red blood cell carrying the protonated hemoglobin reaches the lungs, the proton dissociates from hemoglobin in the presence of atmospheric oxygen which binds to the heme group of hemoglobin. The proton in the red blood cell recombines with the dissolved bicarbonate ion in plasma in the presence of carbonic anhydrase to form the carbonic acid which further dissociates to produce water and carbon dioxide which is then expired (exhaled). In the lungs, carbaminohemoglobin also releases carbon dioxide in the presence of atmospheric oxygen. Oxygen gets into our body by simple diffusion. The atmospheric levels of oxygen therefore cannot produce excess oxygen in the body. Excess carbon dioxide produces excess carbonic acid, and that leads to acidosis which is harmful. The body functions well only within a certain alkaline pH range. There are buffers in the blood that attempt to keep the pH constant. If this approach fails, hyperventilation is provoked to eliminate the excess carbon dioxide . At the same time, the excess proton is being secreted and eliminated through the kidney.
